lead: A parallel program uses p processors to finish sooner than one processor can. Speedup compares the two times, and efficiency says how much of each processor's capacity the work actually uses. These two numbers decide whether buying more cores is worth it. They appear in every parallel benchmark, in cluster job reports, and in cloud bills where you pay per processor-hour. This chapter defines the measures, gives Amdahl's law for the ceiling they impose, and explains what overhead, load imbalance and memory effects do to real measurements.
prereq: You need Chapter 1.1 for why parallelism exists and Chapter 1.3 for where the processors sit.

blocks.text: Let T₁ be the time in seconds for one processor to finish a problem. Let Tₚ be the time in seconds for p processors to finish the same problem. The processor count p is a plain number, at least 1. Speedup compares the two times.

blocks.where: S is speedup (no unit); T₁ is one-processor time in seconds; Tₚ is p-processor time in seconds.

blocks.text: Speedup S answers: how many times faster is the parallel run? If Tₚ = T₁ ÷ p, then S = p. That is perfect linear speedup, and it is the best the basic model allows.
Efficiency divides speedup by the number of processors. It answers: how well is each processor used?

blocks.where: E is efficiency (no unit, often written as a fraction or percentage); S is speedup; p is the processor count; T₁ and Tₚ are times in seconds.

blocks.text: Perfect efficiency is E = 1, or 100 percent. A value of E = 0.6 means each processor does useful work only 60 percent of the time. The rest goes to waiting, communication or idle time.

Cost C = p × Tₚ is the total processor time spent, measured in processor-seconds. Work W = T₁ is the one-processor time, measured in seconds. Their ratio is dimensionless and is exactly the efficiency: E = W ÷ C = T₁ ÷ (p × Tₚ). When E < 1, part of the cost buys no useful work.

blocks.where: C is cost in processor-seconds; p is the processor count; Tₚ is the parallel time in seconds. Work W = T₁ is in seconds.

blocks.text: Some part of a program cannot be parallelised: input reading, a final reduction, a serial loop. Let f be the fraction of the one-processor time spent in that serial part. The parallel part is 1 − f. On p processors, the parallel part can shrink, but the serial part cannot.
Tₚ ≥ f × T₁ + (1 − f) × T₁ ÷ p
blocks.where: f is the serial fraction of T₁ (0 ≤ f ≤ 1); T₁ is one-processor time in seconds; Tₚ is the best possible p-processor time in seconds; p is the processor count.

blocks.text: Divide T₁ by both sides of the inequality. The left side becomes T₁ ÷ Tₚ, which is S, so S ≤ 1 ÷ (f + (1 − f) ÷ p). This is Amdahl's law, an upper bound on speedup.

blocks.where: S(p) is the maximum speedup on p processors; f is the serial fraction; p is the processor count.

blocks.text: As p grows, the term (1 − f) ÷ p goes to zero. The bound approaches 1 ÷ f. A program with f = 0.1 can never exceed speedup 10, however many processors you add. With f = 0.2 the ceiling is 5.

Gustafson's law looks at the other case: the problem size grows with p. If the parallel part expands to fill the extra processors, scaled speedup is S′ = f<sub>G</sub> + p(1 − f<sub>G</sub>). Here f<sub>G</sub> is the serial fraction of the parallel run's time, and f<sub>G</sub> ≠ f in general. The ceiling is no longer 1 ÷ f, because the serial part stays fixed while useful work grows.

Real time Tₚ includes work plus overhead. Overhead is communication between processors, synchronisation at barriers, process startup and message packing. Overhead adds seconds, so it lowers S below the Amdahl bound. A program with perfect load balance can still be slow because of overhead.

Load imbalance means some processors finish early and wait. The slowest processor sets Tₚ. If one processor gets twice the work of the others, adding processors does not help much. Task splitting and load balancing are covered in Chapter 1.7.

Superlinear speedup means S > p. Within the basic formula this is impossible, because Tₚ cannot be less than T₁ ÷ p. It can appear in measurements through cache and memory effects: with p processors each core may hold a larger slice of the data in its private cache, so the parallel run reads less from slow memory. Report such results with the cache explanation, not as a formula result.

Strong scalability fixes the problem size and increases p. Speedup rises, then flattens, and efficiency falls as overhead grows. Weak scalability increases the problem size along with p so that time per processor stays constant. Efficiency near 1 under weak scaling means the machine can handle larger jobs without losing throughput.

figure.caption: Speedup against processor count for the worked example: 20 s of the 200 s run is serial, so f = 0.1. At 8 processors the curve gives 4.71, not the ideal 8, and it flattens towards the hard ceiling of 10.

spec.aria: A plot of speedup against processor count: the ideal line S = p rises straight to 16, the curve for a 10 percent serial fraction rises more slowly and flattens below the flat ceiling line at 10, with a marked point at 8 processors giving speedup 4.71.

examples.question: A program takes 200 s on one processor. Of that time, 20 s is serial and 180 s is parallel. It runs on 8 processors with perfect scaling of the parallel part. Find T₈, the speedup, the efficiency and the maximum speedup as p → ∞. What limits the result?
steps: Serial time = 20 s. Parallel time on one processor = 200 − 20 = 180 s.
On 8 processors the parallel part takes 180 ÷ 8 = 22.5 s.
T₈ = serial time + parallel time = 20 + 22.5 = 42.5 s.
Serial fraction f = 20 ÷ 200 = 0.1. Maximum speedup = 1 ÷ f = 1 ÷ 0.1 = 10.
The serial 20 s sets the ceiling. Real overhead would make T₈ larger than 42.5 s and the speedup smaller than 4.71.
examples.answer: T₈ = 42.5 s, S ≈ 4.71, E ≈ 0.588, and the maximum speedup is 10; the 20 s serial part limits the result.
examples.check:
serial = 20.0
total = 200.0
p = 8
parallel = total - serial
T8 = serial + parallel / p
S = total / T8
E = S / p
limit = 1.0 / (serial / total)
print(T8)
print(round(S, 2))
print(round(E, 3))
print(limit)

traps: Do not report p as the speedup. Speedup is always T₁ ÷ Tₚ, and it can be less than p.
Do not treat the Amdahl bound as a measured result. Overhead and load imbalance make real speedup lower.
Keep units straight: T₁ and Tₚ are seconds, cost is processor-seconds, and S and E have no unit.
A measured speedup above p is not allowed by the formula. Check for cache or memory effects before claiming it.
The serial fraction f is a fraction of one-processor time, not a count of serial lines of code.

quiz.q: Define speedup and efficiency for p processors. Give the symbols and units.
quiz.a: Speedup S = T₁ ÷ Tₚ, where T₁ is one-processor time in seconds and Tₚ is p-processor time in seconds; S has no unit. Efficiency E = S ÷ p = T₁ ÷ (p × Tₚ); E has no unit, and ideal E = 1.

quiz.q: State Amdahl's law and give the limit as p → ∞.
quiz.a: S(p) ≤ 1 ÷ (f + (1 − f) ÷ p), where f is the serial fraction. As p → ∞, the bound tends to 1 ÷ f.

quiz.q: In the basic model, why can efficiency not exceed 1?
quiz.a: Tₚ cannot be smaller than T₁ ÷ p, so S = T₁ ÷ Tₚ ≤ p. Dividing by p gives E = S ÷ p ≤ 1. Overhead and imbalance only make E smaller.

quiz.q: A program takes 120 s on one processor, and 25 percent of that time is serial. Find T₄, S and E on 4 processors, and the maximum speedup.
A program has serial fraction f = 0.05. Find the upper bound on speedup with 16 processors.
A report claims speedup 7.5 on 8 processors. Is this possible? Explain what the number says about efficiency and overhead.
quiz.a: Yes, it is below linear speedup, so the basic formula allows it. E = 7.5 ÷ 8 = 0.9375, so each processor is busy about 94 percent of the time. The gap from 8 comes from the serial part, overhead or slight imbalance. A value above 8 would need a cache or memory explanation.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry performance engineers combine these measures with the roofline model, which plots attained performance against arithmetic intensity and shows whether the peak floating-point rate or memory bandwidth is the binding limit. Profiling tools report time per function, cache misses and communication waits, so you can see whether overhead or imbalance dominates. Cloud autoscaling uses the same strong and weak scaling ideas when it adds virtual machines. Search for "roofline model", "strong versus weak scaling" and "parallel performance profiling" to go further.
